subject.title: Break of Day in the Trenches
subject.author: Isaac Rosenberg
subject.text:
The darkness crumbles away.
It is the same old druid Time as ever,
Only a live thing leaps my hand,
A queer sardonic rat,
As I pull the parapet's poppy
To stick behind my ear.
Droll rat, they would shoot you if they knew
Your cosmopolitan sympathies.
Now you have touched this English hand
You will do the same to a German
Soon, no doubt, if it be your pleasure
To cross the sleeping green between.
It seems you inwardly grin as you pass
Strong eyes, fine limbs, haughty athletes,
Less chanced than you for life,
Bonds to the whims of murder,
Sprawled in the bowels of the earth,
The torn fields of France.
What do you see in our eyes
At the shrieking iron and flame
Hurled through still heavens?
What quaver-what heart aghast?
Poppies whose roots are in man's veins
Drop, and are ever dropping;
But mine in my ear is safe-
Just a little white with the dust.

title: A Rat, a Slur, and a Private's War
standfirst: In the trenches, Isaac Rosenberg gave a scavenging rat the era's coded word for a Jew, and turned an insult into the sharpest line of the First World War's most argued-over poem.

sections.heading: A Rat With the Wrong Kind of Loyalty
sections.body:
Isaac Rosenberg's poem gives its strangest word not to a soldier but to a rat. Watching it scuttle over the parapet at dawn, he calls it droll, then reaches for a phrase that stops most readers cold:

> Droll rat, they would shoot you if they knew
> Your cosmopolitan sympathies.

The rat crosses between the English and German trenches with no preference for either, and it is that indifference — no side, no country — for which Rosenberg picks the era's loaded word.

"Cosmopolitan" was not a neutral adjective in 1916. It was the standard charge against Jews said to hold no fixed national loyalty, an accusation Rosenberg had already met from the inside of his own battalion. In a letter home he wrote plainly that his being a Jew made things bad amongst these wretches.

Read that way, the droll rat starts to look like a self-portrait smuggled past the censor of good taste — the one creature in no-man's-land accused, half-affectionately, of exactly the disloyalty Rosenberg's fellow soldiers accused him of. He does not press the point. He never does. The line sits there, funny and awful at once, and moves on to the poppy.

sections.heading: Chalk on the Pavement
sections.body:
Rosenberg was born in Bristol in 1890, the second of six children of Barnett and Hacha Rosenberg, Lithuanian Jewish immigrants who had fled Tsarist Dvinsk. The family moved to Stepney in 1897, into one of the poorest corners of London's East End, and stayed poor. He left school at fourteen to apprentice with the engraver Carl Hentschel, work he disliked, and drew in evening classes at Birkbeck College because there was nowhere else to draw. According to his biographer Jean Moorcroft Wilson, the family's poverty ran so deep that Rosenberg found his first canvases to be the East End pavements where he drew in chalk.

He was rescued, if that is the word, in March 1911: a chance meeting at the National Gallery led to Lily Delissa Joseph and a circle of wealthier, more established Anglo-Jewish women, one of whom sponsored his place at the Slade School of Fine Art that autumn. He arrived among classmates who would become the era's major names — David Bomberg, Mark Gertler, Paul Nash, Stanley Spencer — as a scholarship boy funded by charity, a poet nobody there had asked for.

sections.heading: A Private Among the Patrons
sections.body:
By the time he reached the Slade, Rosenberg had found the other half of his world: the loose circle of East End Jewish artists and writers who gathered around Whitechapel Library and the Whitechapel Gallery, and called themselves, half-joking, the Whitechapel Boys. Bomberg, Gertler and the poet John Rodker were part of it; more distantly, so was the patron and Georgian Poetry editor Edward Marsh, who took an interest in Rosenberg's verse from 1913 and stayed in correspondence with him through the war, alongside the playwright Gordon Bottomley and the poet Laurence Binyon.

That correspondence kept his poetry alive in London while he was in France, but it did not make him one of his patrons' world. He had no private income, no officer's commission, no Oxford or Cambridge behind him. When he enlisted in October 1915 it was not for King and country: "I never joined the army for patriotic reasons," he wrote. "Nothing can justify war. I suppose we must all fight to get the trouble over." He joined because a private soldier's separation allowance would go straight to his mother. He was posted first to a Bantam battalion, raised for men under the regulation height, and later transferred into the King's Own Royal Lancaster Regiment. Sassoon and Wilfred Owen held commissions; Rosenberg carried a rifle and dug.

sections.heading: The Un-Aubade
sections.body:
"Break of Day in the Trenches" is, formally, a joke at the expense of an old genre. The aubade is the poem of parting lovers at sunrise; Rosenberg takes its title moment, the crumbling dark, and empties it of everything but a soldier, a rat and a flower pulled from the parapet. The twenty-six lines run on as a single unbroken block, unrhymed, and the first line opens in what sounds like a steady iambic beat before the pattern gives way a few syllables later — the darkness, formally as well as literally, crumbles.

Sending the poem to Marsh from the trenches, Rosenberg [called it "as simple as ordinary talk"](https://war.web.ox.ac.uk/break-day-trenches-hypermedia-edition), and pre-empted criticism of one line himself: "you might object to the second line as vague, but that was the best way I could express the sense of dawn."

An earlier draft, made before the text reached *Poetry* magazine, carried an extra line at the point where the poem turns to the "torn fields of France" — naming, in so many words, "what antipathies" lay behind the slaughter. Cutting it was the harder, better choice. It leaves cosmopolitan sympathies to carry the poem's politics alone, unglossed, so a reader has to notice the loaded word rather than being told to.

sections.heading: Second to Owen
sections.body:
Rosenberg sent "Break of Day in the Trenches" to Harriet Monroe's *Poetry* magazine in Chicago in October 1916, apologising that he had no means of knowing, or seeing your magazine out here. It appeared that December — his only real publication of the poem in his lifetime. He did not live to see it collected: *Poems*, edited by Gordon Bottomley with an introductory memoir by Laurence Binyon, did not appear until 1922, four years after his death. Binyon's memoir is affectionate and a little startled by its own subject, describing a man "small in stature, dark, bright-eyed, thoroughly Jewish in type," with "an unusual mixture of self-reliance and modesty" — the tone of someone still working out how seriously to take a private soldier's poems.

The critic Bernard Bergonzi later called Rosenberg "undoubtedly one of the finest poets that the Great War produced," and Paul Fussell, in *The Great War and Modern Memory*, went further and named this poem "the greatest poem of the war" — a claim still argued over rather than settled. Yet Rosenberg has never had Wilfred Owen's fame, or Sassoon's, or Rupert Brooke's; critics who rank him with or above them tend to be making an argument, not reporting a consensus. Where Owen's poems reach for pity and Sassoon's for anger, Rosenberg's trench poems keep a stranger, more detached humour — droll is his own word for the rat, and it fits him too.

sections.heading: Fampoux, 1 April 1918
sections.body:
The Germans launched their spring offensive on 21 March 1918. Rosenberg's last surviving letter, enclosing the poem "Through These Pale Cold Days," went out before he returned to the front line. On the night of 1 April, after completing a patrol near Fampoux, northeast of Arras, he was killed alongside ten other men of the King's Own Royal Lancaster Regiment; accounts differ on whether it was a sniper or a close-range encounter, and the difference has never been settled. He was twenty-seven.

His body was not identified at the time. The remains of eleven King's Own Royal Lancaster soldiers, found together in 1926, were reburied at Bailleul Road East Cemetery at Saint-Laurent-Blangy; Rosenberg's headstone there gives no individual grave, only his name and, unusually for a private soldier's stone, the description "Artist and Poet." In November 1985 his name was added, with fifteen other poets of the war, to a slate memorial in Westminster Abbey's Poets' Corner — recognition that arrived sixty-seven years after the East End engraver's apprentice, who had paid his patrons in poems rather than deference, stopped being able to write any more of them.
